Comprising more than 280,000 artifacts, the finds—uncovered between modern-day Cambridge and Huntingdon —shed light on life in the region over roughly 12,000 years. But some discoveries raised more questions than answers: Why, for example, did a single ditch at the Bar Hill site in rural Cambridgeshire contain some 8,000 amphibian bones ? pages.text: Are Humans the Only Species to Drive Others to Extinction? And More Questions From Our Readers Skip to main content Are humans the only species to drive another to extinction? Illustration by Aitch Are humans the only species to drive another to extinction? Tom Ruppel | Dixon, California Human activities are the most prominent cause of species extinction today, but not the only one. A recent study estimated that over half of contemporary extinctions in land vertebrates were caused, at least in part, by invasive species. The domestic cat is among the worst offenders; its cuteness belies how devastatingly effective it is at hunting birds and small mammals. The cat’s influence has been most severe on islands where native species evolved without predators and therefore have no defenses. One can assign humans some of the blame for introducing predators. However, the fossil record shows that species have been going extinct for far longer than humans have been around. Some extinctions were caused by changes in the physical environment, such as the asteroid impact that killed off the dinosaurs (except for birds). However, many other species have gone extinct when nothing dramatic seemed to be happening. Some of these surely were related to the effects of predators, parasites and competitors—though the fossil record generally doesn’t give us enough information to identify the cause of a species’ demise. — Gene Hunt, curator of paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History Why did Grover Cleveland lose his first re-election bid but win again four years later? Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Black Mountain Herd Management Area (HMA) Descendants of burros brought by miners and prospectors from the early 1860s. These burros are of North African ancestry. Location: The Black Mountain Herd Management Area (HMA) is in extreme northwestern Arizona, 15 miles west of Kingman. The area parallels the eastern shoreline of the Colorado River for 80 miles, from Hoover Dam south to the Needles Bridge in California. The historic gold mining town of Oatman lies in the center of the southern half of the HMA, along Historic Route 66. Size: Black Mountain is the largest HMA in Arizona, with about 1.1 million acres of Mojave Desert shrub and Grand Canyon desert shrub. Topography/Vegetation: This region is volcanic in origin, resulting in an area that is characterized by large mesas, steep cliffs, slopes, rocky foothills, alluvial fans and sandy washes. The climate is hot, windy and dry, with summertime temperatures exceeding 120 degrees. The winter lows can be 25 degrees. pages.text: Armenia's Long-Distance Trail Runs More Than 500 Miles Past Ancient Monasteries | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD Why Armenia Is Becoming an Adventure Traveler’s Dream Destination Ongoing improvements to the Transcaucasian Trail mean that the best way to experience the country’s natural beauty and rich cultural history is on foot. Since 2017, the Transcaucasian Trail has connected Lake Parz, in Dilijan National Park, with the spa town of Dilijan to the west. Anush Babajanyan By Alicia Erickson Published October 20, 2026 Volcanic peaks. Silk Road–era guesthouses. Homemade cheese and apricot brandy after a day of hiking. All of this awaits visitors to the Armenian section of the Transcaucasian Trail (TCT), which stretches more than 500 miles from Meghri on the country’s southern border to Lake Arpi National Park in the north, winding through oak forests, deep river gorges, and remote mountain villages. Built largely by volunteers beginning in 2016, the TCT reconnects historic footpaths and shepherds' routes across the Caucasus. When it is completed sometime in the next decade, the trail will span 1,864 miles across Armenia, Georgia, and Azerbaijan. New downloadable maps, improved trails and signage, and expanded trekking services rolling out through 2027 will make it easier than ever to explore Armenia on foot. Despite these improvements, many sections of the trail see only a handful of hikers, allowing travelers to wander through dramatic landscapes and remote communities without the crowds.
